why: The ONE selection merge vocabulary of the framework interaction contract, written once and read by every implementation: the Rust reducer (`next_selection`, 🧰️framework/🔨️modules/📡️replication/📡️wire/🦀️.rs), the Rust domain path (the reserved `interactionSelect` job's `parse_merge_mode`, 🧰️framework/🛍️products/💻️os/🔨️modules/🔌️plugin/🦀️.rs), the non-domain world path (`merge_world_selection_ids`/`merge_string_ids`), the TypeScript reducer (`nextSelection`, 🕹️interaction/🟦️.ts), and every renderer host that builds an `interactionSelect` wire arg. The words are NOT a host convention: they are the `MergeMode` enum of this module's own schema, and `schema.$defs` below is the authority both twins validate against.
liveDefect: Ticket 26/09/09/PROCEDURAL-3D-END-TO-END, 2026-09-12 (`📓️selection-dedupe-2026-09-12.md` §6, `📓️selection-merge-vocabulary-2026-09-12.md`): TWO vocabularies were in the tree. `World3dHost`'s `instanceMergeArg`/`componentMergeArg` translated the resolved `MergeMode` into `add`/`remove`/`toggle`/`replace`, while the framework's `parse_merge_mode` accepts only the five schema words and faults `interactionSelect: unknown merge '…'` on anything else. So every shift-click / ctrl-click on a DOMAIN-BOUND world scene (the generation3d preview) faulted, and only the unmodified `replace` pick worked. The `add`/`remove`/`toggle` words were the non-domain `worldPick`/`worldVortexSelect` path's own private spelling of the same three set operations. They are DELETED, not adapted — greenfield, no compatibility layer.

schema.why: Schema-first: the vocabulary is generated from, and re-validated against, this module's owned schema export — not re-typed per implementation.

modifierPolicy.why: The ONE modifier→merge map of a world viewport, unchanged from `marqueeModeFromModifiers` (🖱️ui react target) — this fixture only renames what the host then puts on the wire, never which mode a chord resolves to. `pick` is a whole-instance pick or a marquee drag; `componentPick` is the vertex/edge/face pick, whose bare click TOGGLES (a component pick is a paint-like accumulate gesture, not a replace). Neither ever produces `range`: a world viewport has no ordered topology for a shift-drag to span, which is why shift is additive here and `range` belongs to ordered surfaces (`interactionMergeFromModifiers`, Tree rows).

topology.why: The ordered node list a `range` merge spans — `DomainTopology.ordered`'s sequence IS the range order (pre-order), and it is the only thing that gives `range` a meaning.

range.decision: ACCEPTED, not rejected — `range` stays in the vocabulary and is defined for every domain that declares an ordered topology.
range.law: The anchor is `current.anchorId`, falling back to the last id of the current selection, falling back to the batch's last target. The result is the INCLUSIVE slice of `DomainTopology.ordered` between the anchor's index and the last target's index, in topology order whichever way the pair runs; the published `anchorId` stays the anchor, so a second shift-click from the same anchor re-spans rather than walking.
range.unorderedDomains: When the topology orders NEITHER endpoint (an empty `ordered`, a target the app's `interaction_topology` does not report), `range` degrades to a single-target pick of the batch's last target, which becomes the new anchor. This is a defined outcome, not a fault: `range` is a legal word on every domain, and a domain that publishes no order simply has no span to take. A world3d viewport is exactly that case — which is why its modifier map never emits `range` in the first place (see `modifierPolicy.neverEmitted`), so the degradation is a safety net for a programmatic dispatch, not a gesture anyone can perform.

cases.why: A plain pick replaces: the previous selection is gone, and the picked id is the new anchor.
A selection is a SET: several rendered instances of one topology id picked in one batch select it once.
Shift-click on a world scene: the picked id joins the set, in first-seen order, and becomes the anchor.
`Select` is event-sourced: re-adding an already selected id is a no-op, never a second entry.
Ctrl/cmd-click on a world scene: the picked id leaves the set and the rest keeps its order.
Removing what was never selected changes nothing — the anchor still moves to the picked id.
Shift+ctrl-click on a world scene: a selected id leaves, an unselected id joins, in ONE batch.
The inclusive topology-order slice from the anchor to the target, and the anchor is KEPT so a second range pick re-spans from the same origin.
A target BEFORE the anchor spans the same slice — always in topology order, never in gesture order.
A selection that carries no explicit anchor (a programmatic seed, a restored session) still ranges — from the last id it holds.

The decision in `range.unorderedDomains`: a domain whose topology orders neither endpoint has no span to take, so `range` picks the last target alone and re-anchors there — a defined outcome, never a fault.

wiring.why: Source-level anchors both twins re-check, so no implementation can reintroduce a private spelling of these five words — which is exactly how the live defect was introduced.
